title: Arise, Go Up to Bethel — Put Away, Rename, Bury
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace to you. I want to begin with a question: where is your Bethel?

What I mean is this — somewhere along the road of your faith, was there a moment when you met God unmistakably? It might have been in the back row at an evangelistic meeting. It might have been in a hospital corridor. It might have been on some night nobody else knew about. On that occasion you said some things to God; you made a vow, you settled a resolve. And then life went on moving forward, and those words are still there — you have simply not taken them out and looked at them for a very long time.

Genesis 35 opens with God saying, "Arise, go up to Bethel." And the timing of that sentence deserves our very closest attention — it comes just as the catastrophe of chapter 34 has finished playing itself out. A daughter had been violated, the sons had put a whole city to the sword, and the stink of it was on the entire household. At the moment when this family looked least like anything, God opens his mouth and says: get up, we are going there now.
"God said to Jacob, 'Arise, go up to Bethel, and live there. Make there an altar to God, who appeared to you when you fled from the face of Esau your brother.'" (Genesis 35:1)
There are three verbs in this one verse, and each one lands heavier than the one before.
The first is "arise", קוּם (*qum*). Thirty years earlier, Isaac had used this very word to send him away. Every turning point in a life, more often than not, begins with somebody saying, "Arise."

The second is "go up", עֲלֵה (*aleh*). Bethel stands in the hill country, so the movement is upward. All through the Bible, coming before God is a climb. You do not stumble into Bethel by accident; you have to decide to walk up that slope.

The third is "live there", וְשֶׁב־שָׁם (*veshev-sham*). That is the key word. Thirty years ago he was only passing through — one night's sleep with a stone under his head, on the run. This time God says: settle down and stay.

Brothers and sisters, a great many people have a passing-through kind of spiritual life. One conference, once. One retreat, once. Moved once, wept once — and then back to exactly where they were before. What God says here is: stop passing through. Live there.

And notice how God introduces himself in verse 1: "who appeared to you when you fled from the face of Esau your brother." The Hebrew is בְּבָרְחֲךָ (*bevorchacha*) — "in your fleeing", at the time when you were running away.

God could perfectly well have said, "the One who made heaven and earth", or "the God of your father Abraham." Instead he picked out the most undignified moment of Jacob's whole life to introduce himself by. Because that was the moment when Jacob really came to know him.

Have you noticed this — that the stretch of our story we most dread anyone bringing up is very often the stretch God treasures most? The flight we would like to forget is the place God takes for his landmark.

And one more thing. Thirty years ago at Bethel, Jacob set up nothing but a pillar; this time God says, "Make there an altar." A pillar is a monument; an altar is a place where something is handed over. A pillar says, "I met God here." An altar says, "I gave something up here." Between the monument and the offering lie thirty years.
Why did God pick this particular moment to tell him to go up to Bethel?

The timing is the most moving thing in the whole chapter. The catastrophe of chapter 34 has only just ended — a daughter violated, the sons putting a city to the sword, the stink of it on the whole household; and at the moment when this family looked least like anything, God says, "Arise, go up to Bethel." God does not wait until a household has been tidied up before he calls it home. He speaks in the middle of the mess. And the way he introduces himself is as the One "who appeared to you when you fled from the face of Esau your brother" — he picks out the most undignified moment of Jacob's life. The stretch of our story we most dread anyone bringing up is very often the very place God takes for his landmark.
What is different about "live there", compared with thirty years ago?

Thirty years ago he was only passing through — one night's sleep with a stone under his head, on the run; this time what God says is, live there. A great many people have a passing-through kind of spiritual life: one conference, one retreat, moved once, wept once, and then back to exactly where they were before. And there is a second contrast that is even plainer. Thirty years ago what he set up was a pillar; this time God says, "Make there an altar." A pillar is a monument, and it says, "I met God here"; an altar is a place of sacrifice, and it says, "I gave something up here." Between the monument and the offering lie thirty years. If your Bethel has stopped at the monument, it is worth asking yourself: where is the altar?
2. Put Away, Purify Yourselves, Change Your Garments
God spoke one sentence, and Jacob answered it with three actions:
"Put away the foreign gods that are among you, purify yourselves, and change your garments." (Genesis 35:2)
"Put away" is הָסִרוּ (*hasiru*), a Hiphil, and it means "cause it to be gone" — not put it out of sight, but take it away.

"The foreign gods" is אֱלֹהֵי הַנֵּכָר (*elohei hanechar*). Brothers and sisters, do the arithmetic: Rachel stole her father's household gods back in chapter 31. How many years lie between chapter 31 and chapter 35? All that time those images have been riding along in this family's luggage.
They have been to Peniel. They have been reconciled with Esau. They have built an altar — they have even given that altar a name, El-Elohe-Israel. And those images are still there.

We are exactly the same. We can worship, we can serve, we can share in the small group with real light on our faces — and all the while there is one thing in the luggage that has never been handed over. It makes no noise and gives no trouble. It simply sits there. Until one day something goes wrong in the family, and we discover it has been there the whole time.

"Purify yourselves" (וְהִטַּהֲרוּ, *vehittaharu*) and "change your garments" (וְהַחֲלִיפוּ שִׂמְלֹתֵיכֶם, *vehachalifu simloteichem*) are the very same set of preparations God would later command Moses to have the people carry out before they came up to Sinai. Which is to say: what Jacob's household did that day was a small, domestic version of getting ready to meet God.
Verse 4 holds a very moving detail: "They gave to Jacob all the foreign gods which were in their hands, and the rings which were in their ears; and Jacob hid them under the oak which was by Shechem."
"Hid" is וַיִּטְמֹן (*vayitmon*), and that word is normally used for burying. He did not throw them away; he buried them. A thing thrown away can still be fished back out. A thing buried is dead.

And he buried them at Shechem — the very city where the blood was shed in the previous chapter, the very place where he should have moved on and stopped instead. At the address of his own failure he dug a hole, put those things into it, and then took the road.

Brothers and sisters, before you go back to Bethel there has to be a subtraction. There are things which, left unburied, will keep you off that mountain. Not because God is unwilling to take you up, but because you cannot climb with that on your back.

Verse 5: "They traveled, and a terror of God was on the cities that were around them, and they didn't pursue the sons of Jacob." The Hebrew is חִתַּת אֱלֹהִים (*chittat elohim*), literally a dread that comes from God.

By any ordinary reckoning, after a city has been put to the sword the whole district comes looking for revenge. But nobody moved. When you take the step of obedience, the obstacles along that road are very often handled by God himself. That is not your cleverness. That is his guard around you.
Those images sat there all the way from chapter 31 to chapter 35. Why did it drag on so long?

That is exactly the most unnerving thing about it. In between, they went to Peniel, they were reconciled with Esau, they built an altar and even gave the altar a name — and those images were still in the luggage. We are the same: we can worship, we can serve, we can share in the small group with real light on our faces, and all the while one thing in the luggage has never been handed over. It makes no noise and gives no trouble; it simply sits there, until something goes wrong at home and we find it has been there the whole time. Which is why a regular subtraction is necessary — not a clear-out after the disaster, but a question asked every so often: is there anything in my hand that I have never been willing to bring out?
He "hid" the images under the oak. What does that word carry?

The Hebrew word is normally used for burying — he did not throw them away, he buried them. A thing thrown away can still be fished back out; a thing buried is dead. And the place he buried them was Shechem: the city where the blood was shed in the previous chapter, the place where he should have moved on and stopped instead. At the address of his own failure he dug a hole, put those things in, and then took the road. That picture is intensely practical for us. The best place to deal with a thing is the place where it went wrong, and it has to be dealt with to the point of no return — deleted, cancelled, replaced, told to another person. Leave yourself a way back, and that thing is still alive.
3. A Light from the Original: God Appeared to Him Again, and Fixed the Name with His Own Mouth
Verse 9: "God appeared to Jacob again, when he came from Paddan Aram, and blessed him."
"Again" — the Hebrew is עוֹד (*od*). This is Bethel a second time. In the same place, to the same man, God speaks a second time.
Verse 10: "Your name is Jacob. Your name shall not be Jacob any more, but your name will be Israel."

Notice the order in which God speaks. First he acknowledges the old name: "Your name is Jacob." He does not pretend those thirty years never happened; he does not pretend the heel-grabber never existed. God never denies your past in order to hand you a new identity.

Then he says, "Your name shall not be Jacob any more" — and the Hebrew there, לֹא־יִקָּרֵא (*lo yiqqare*), is passive: "shall no longer be called." At Peniel that new name came in the dark, and he was the only one who heard it. At Bethel God confirms it in the open. From now on it is not only that he knows it; everyone is to call him by it.

Brothers and sisters, plenty of people have had a Peniel experience — a night of wrestling with God, and a new name at the end of it. But when daylight comes back, they go on living under the old name. What you need is a Bethel. You need that new name publicly, formally settled.

Verse 11: "I am God Almighty." The Hebrew is אֲנִי אֵל שַׁדַּי (*ani El Shaddai*). God spoke this name to Abraham (17:1), and Isaac used it when he blessed Jacob (28:3); now God says it to Jacob with his own mouth. The third generation has finally heard it for himself.
Faith cannot be lived on an inheritance. The God of your parents has one day to become your own God.

The promise that follows uses a very old pair of verbs: "Be fruitful and multiply" (פְּרֵה וּרְבֵה, *pereh urveh*) — which is precisely the first blessing God ever spoke over human beings, back in Genesis 1. In a household where a life has only just been taken, God says again the sentence he said at the beginning of creation. That is what grace is like: he starts over from the top.

Then God adds a sentence Genesis has never contained before: "kings will come out of your body" (מְלָכִים, *melachim*). For the first time in Genesis, kingship is promised out of this line. And the word behind "a company of nations" is קָהָל (*qahal*), which the Septuagint renders ἐκκλησία — church.
In this least presentable of households, God speaks out the prophecy of the church and of the king ahead of time.

In verse 14 Jacob "set up a pillar in the place where he spoke with him, a pillar of stone. He poured out a drink offering on it, and poured oil on it." Thirty years ago he set up a pillar too, and poured oil too; this time there is one thing more — the drink offering. A drink offering means tipping a whole flask onto the ground and keeping not one drop for yourself.

Thirty years ago he was a man striking a bargain — "If God will be with me … of all that you will give me I will surely give a tenth to you." Thirty years later he is a man pouring himself out. Maturity in the spiritual life is the distance between haggling and emptying the flask.
God says, "Your name is Jacob. Your name shall not be Jacob any more" — why bring up the old name first?

Because God never denies your past in order to hand you a new identity. He acknowledges the old name first; he does not pretend those thirty years never happened. And "your name shall not be Jacob any more" is passive in the Hebrew — literally, "shall no longer be called." At Peniel that new name came in the dark and he was the only one who heard it; at Bethel God confirms it in the open. Plenty of people have had a Peniel experience — a night of wrestling with God and a new name at the end of it — and then daylight comes back and they go on living under the old name. What you need is a Bethel: let that new name be formally settled, and let other people call you by it.
4. Burials, and the Names Nobody Can Bring Themselves to Say
There are three funerals in this chapter.

The first is Deborah, Rebekah's nurse. She died, and was buried below Bethel under the oak, and the tree was named Allon Bacuth — the oak of weeping. An old servant with no rank and no standing, and Scripture records her name and records the name of the tree over her grave. God never overlooks the small people.
The second is Rachel. "They traveled from Bethel. There was still some distance to come to Ephrath, and Rachel travailed. She had hard labor." (Genesis 35:16)

"Hard" is וַתְּקַשׁ (*vateqash*), from a root meaning hard, difficult. The midwife said to her, "Don't be afraid, for now you will have another son" — the only time in the whole chapter that anybody says "don't be afraid" to a woman. And she died all the same.
"As her soul was departing (for she died), she named him Benoni, but his father named him Benjamin." (Genesis 35:18)
Ben-oni, בֶּן־אוֹנִי (*Ben-oni*), means "son of my sorrow". With her last breath the mother wrote her own pain into her child's name.

The father would not let that name stand. He renamed him Benjamin, בִנְיָמִין (*Binyamin*) — "son of the right hand". In Scripture the right hand is the place of strength, of honour, of being received with favour.

Brothers and sisters, this is the gentlest thing Jacob ever did in his life. He did not deny Rachel's pain — the pillar over her grave stands there, and the text says it is there "to this day". But he would not let this child carry his mother's pain as his name for the rest of his life.

Suffering is real, but suffering does not have to become your name. You can be "the one God loves" rather than "the one who was thrown away"; you can be the son of the right hand rather than the son of sorrow. Renaming is not a denial of the past. It is a refusal to let the past define your future for you.

And look where this happened: Ephrath — which is Bethlehem. Micah 5 says, "But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, being small among the clans of Judah, out of you one will come out to me who is to be ruler in Israel."

Seventeen hundred years later, in that same small town, another mother gave birth to a son. And that one willingly became Ben-oni — the son of sorrow — so that all of us might become Benjamin, and sit in the place at the right hand.

There is a third funeral in this chapter: Isaac's. "Isaac gave up the spirit and died, and was gathered to his people, old and full of days. Esau and Jacob, his sons, buried him." Since the day in chapter 27 when the blessing was stolen away, these two brothers have at last done one thing together.

Except that, wedged in between those three funerals, is the single sentence of verse 22: "While Israel lived in that land, Reuben went and lay with Bilhah, his father's concubine, and Israel heard of it."

The text says only that he "heard of it". Silence again. The sickness of the previous chapter has not cleared up in this one. And the account this verse opens is not settled until chapter 49 — the birthright of the firstborn was lost on this day.
The father changed "Ben-oni" into "Benjamin". Does that count as denying the mother's pain?

It does not, and in fact this is the gentlest thing Jacob ever did in his life. He did not erase Rachel's pain — the pillar over her grave stands there, and the text says it is there "to this day". He simply would not let this child carry his mother's pain as his name for the rest of his life. Ben-oni means "son of my sorrow"; Benjamin means "son of the right hand", and in Scripture the right hand is the place of strength, of honour, of being received with favour. This gives us a distinction that matters enormously: suffering is real, but suffering does not have to become your name. Renaming is not a denial of the past; it is a refusal to let the past define your future for you. And notice where it happened — at Ephrath, which is Bethlehem.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot
Preach this chapter carelessly and it goes off the road very easily. There are several places you have to be able to recognise.

The first distortion is preaching "go up to Bethel" as a return to some location, some conference, some style of meeting. Bethel stands for that covenant relationship, not for a venue. Preach it as a place and the congregation will go chasing a feeling, and when the chase is over they will go back to the life they had. The test is this: when they have heard you, do they go back to their relationship with God, or do they go looking for another conference?

The second distortion is preaching the putting away of idols without preaching that God spoke first. Verse 1 is God speaking; only in verse 2 does Jacob act. That order cannot be reversed. Reverse it and this chapter becomes a programme of self-improvement running on willpower. The test is this: when the congregation walks out, are they leaning on their own resolve, or on the God who came looking for them first?

The third distortion is preaching Rachel's death as a punishment for some deficiency in Jacob's obedience. She died on the road of obedience. Obedience is no guarantee of a road without tears. Preach it as punishment and you will double the self-reproach of every obedient person who is suffering right now — and that is the one mistake this chapter must never be made to commit.

The fourth distortion is skipping the verse about Reuben. It is a single sentence, and it bears its fruit in chapter 49. Skip it and the congregation never learns the most necessary sentence of all: what goes undealt with detonates later.

The fifth distortion is preaching the burial of the idols as something settled once and for all. What Jacob buried was that journey's luggage; by chapter 49 the trouble in his household is still there. Spiritual subtraction is not one emptying-out; it is a clearing that goes on all along the road. What you bury this year may well grow a fresh one next year.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question. In our homes there are very often things we are too embarrassed to throw out. It is not that we still believe in them: an elder gave it to us, it came along in a house move, it does no harm to keep it. Some of them are objects, some are customs, some are rules nobody can quite explain. Brothers and sisters, I am not telling you to pick a fight with your family, and I am not telling you to dispose of an elder's belongings behind their back. What I am saying is that you must clear the place in your own heart before God, and then talk it through with wisdom and with love. Jacob did not go rummaging through the bags himself either; he said it out loud and let the whole household hand things over of their own accord. What you have to do is open the conversation first, and then be the first one to hand something over.

The second question. We are very good at giving our children names of sorrow. Not necessarily names on a document — the labels that hang perpetually on our lips: "you're just no good", "nobody in our family was ever cut out for studying", "you're exactly like your father." The Ben-oni the mother left behind was changed by one sentence from the father. This week, could you change one? Change one sentence you say to your child. Change one label you have hung on your husband or your wife. And change the name you have been calling yourself for years. The first thing God did at Bethel was to give a man a new name.
I do have a Bethel, but it was many years ago now. Can I still get back there?

You can, and this chapter tells you how. First, you do not get back on a wave of emotion — Jacob walked a road and climbed a slope to get there, so fix a time and a place and treat it as a real appointment. Second, before you go there has to be a subtraction: deal with that one thing you have never been willing to hand over, because you cannot climb with it on your back. Third, going back is not reliving the feeling; it is building an altar — write down one concrete thing you are handing over. Fourth, let one person know you have done it. And if you feel you have been cold for a very long time, this chapter is exactly the one for you: God spoke first.
7. Living 321 Out — Back to the Place Where the Covenant Was Made
Brothers and sisters, let us take this lesson back to the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model. When God said, "Arise, go up to Bethel", a life had only just been taken in this household. And what the Lord Jesus says to the church in Ephesus is the same sentence: "Remember therefore from where you have fallen, and repent and do the first works." My role model is this: he always goes first to the one who is in no fit state. So I too am to go first to the one who is in no fit state — myself included.

The Bible is my standard. Not waiting until I feel worthy enough to go back, but getting up on the day I hear. Feeling says, "when I am a little better." The standard says, "today." The definition of turning back is not that I return once I have improved somewhat; it is that I get up on the very day I hear.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. Which thing is to be buried, and when it is to be buried, is what the Holy Spirit shines his light on. Take your own inventory and you will end up with a long list of guilt; when the Holy Spirit shines, he usually gives you one thing only, and he gives it very concretely. Rely on our intellect and on ourselves, and we worry; rely on the heart and on the Holy Spirit, and we are glad.

Let Jesus be King. "Put away the foreign gods that are among you" — before Jesus can be King, room has to be cleared. A king does not share a house with idols. There are things which, left unburied, will keep you off that mountain.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. Thirty years ago he set up a pillar to commemorate his own meeting with God; thirty years later he pours out a drink offering — the whole flask emptied, not one drop kept back. Giving the glory to God is not adding "praise the Lord" at the end of a sentence. It is tipping that flask over.

Establish God's system. At Bethel God restates the name Israel and speaks of a nation, of a company of nations, of kings, and of that word which would later be translated "church". God's system is set going again at the place where the covenant was made — not out of human resources, but out of the sentence God says over again.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One Road Up the Mountain
We come to this chapter carrying four kinds of heart.

The proud heart says, "Bethel? I went there long ago." Yes, you did. But on that occasion you only set up a pillar; you never built an altar. You passed through; you never settled there. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights — treating one experience as a permanent credential. Humility is returning to our originally intended position as human beings and admitting that I need to make that climb again.

The fearful heart says, "In the state I am in, how would I dare go back?" Brothers and sisters, the moment God chose to speak was the moment this family looked least like anything. He does not wait until you have tidied yourself up before he calls you home. He calls you home, and then he does the tidying there.

The ashamed heart says, "He must never want to mention me again." But he did mention it — he said, the One "who appeared to you when you fled from the face of Esau your brother". He brings up your most undignified moment himself, and not in order to shame you. He does it to tell you: I was there the whole time.

The wounded heart says, "I obeyed — so why did I still lose?" Rachel died on the road of obedience. I cannot give you a tidy explanation. All I can do is tell you what the text says: on that road there is a gravestone, and there is also a child called the son of the right hand; and in that same small town there was later born a Saviour who carried every one of our sorrows for us.
Four kinds of heart, one road up the mountain. And God says the same sentence to all four: Arise, go up to Bethel.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, towards God. Write down what you once said to God — the vow, the resolve, the sentence that began, "Lord, if you will … then I will …" Write it out, look at it, and see which line has never been honoured.
Second, towards yourself. Ask the Holy Spirit for one thing, just one: what is to be buried this week? Do not work it up into a long inventory. One is enough — and then actually deal with it.

Third, towards people. Lead your family in making one spiritual decision together, the way Jacob gathered his whole household. It could be praying together once; it could be dealing with one matter together. You speak first, and you hand something over first.

Fourth, towards daily living. Change one name. It might be a verdict you have passed on your child; it might be the sentence you have been saying to yourself for twenty years. From today, stop calling yourself Ben-oni.
Fifth, towards your calling. Go back to the plainness of your first serving, and do once more the thing you did at the beginning — that small task nobody saw, the one with no title attached to it.

Sixth, tell it to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First: I once met God unmistakably, and afterwards I drifted a long way off. Second: what I found is that the part of me he remembers is exactly my most undignified stretch. Third: so I have decided to go back — not to wait until I have improved and then go back.
Brothers and sisters, let us make our declaration together before God:
I declare that I will no longer pass through Bethel; I will live there.
I declare that I will bury what needs burying, and clear the room so that Jesus may be King.
I declare that suffering is no longer my name; I am the son of the right hand, the one God loves.
I declare that on the day I hear, I will arise; I will not wait until I am better before I come back to God.
This week's family clear-out — how do I actually lead it so that it does not turn into everybody inspecting everybody else?

Three principles. First, begin with yourself: the parent, the leader, names his own one thing to be buried before anyone else's name is mentioned. Second, make it clear that this is not an audit of other people's luggage — do not demand that family members hand over their phones, and do not let anyone drag up old scores; that turns a clear-out into an interrogation. Third, do one thing together: the whole family throwing out one object, agreeing on one new rhythm for the day, going to one place to pray. What Jacob's household did that day was one shared action, not mutual policing. And if your family are unwilling to take part, do it yourself first and do not force them; your own obedience is the best invitation there is.

Thirty years ago, a young man on the run fell asleep in open country with a stone under his head and dreamed of a stairway. He got up, set up a pillar and said, "How awesome this place is! This is none other than God's house." And then he left.

Thirty years later he comes back to the same place with eleven sons, a body full of scars and a past with blood in it. This time he builds an altar, empties out the wine, and buries what was in the luggage. And there God says to him: your name is Israel.

So the focus is on Jesus — not on myself, not on other people, not on my circumstances. Not I, but Christ. The road back was not one I found for myself; he opened his mouth and told me to arise. That new name was not one I earned; he gave it with his own mouth. And even the people along that road who by rights should have hunted me down — he was the one who held them back.

May God bless every one of us to actually arise this week and go up to Bethel; may we bury what needs burying, pour out what needs pouring out, and change that name of sorrow; and may we no longer merely pass through the house of God, but live in it, until we see his face. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson never gets past mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★★ A pillar says, "I met God here"; an altar says, "I gave something up here." Which of the two has your Bethel stopped at?
2. ★★ They had worshipped, they had been reconciled, they had built an altar — and the images were in the luggage the whole time. What is that telling us?
3. ★ God acknowledges the old name before he gives the new one. What does that say to the idea that once you believe you should never mention the past again?
4. ★★ Suffering is real, but suffering does not have to become your name. How does that sentence apply to you?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I went through all that long ago), fearful (I am afraid that if I hand that one thing over I will have nothing left), ashamed (what is in my luggage cannot be said out loud), wounded (my name is "son of sorrow"). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "Arise, go up to Bethel, and live there." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Where is your Bethel? What did you say to God on that occasion, and does it still stand today?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "The thing in my luggage that still has not been buried is …"
9. ★★ This week, on which day and in what place will you go back to your Bethel once? Say the time out loud.

Leader's reminder: the questions in this section may touch loss, and years of self-reproach over having gone cold. Do not say, "How could you have let it drag on this long?" If someone speaks of losing a family member, or of losing a child in a difficult birth, stay with him first, and follow up with him privately after the meeting.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your home, is there one thing the whole family could bury together? Say how you will open the conversation.
11. ★ The same question in another setting: in your serving or at your work, which habit is the one that should be taken away?

12. ★★★ The renaming practice: this week, write down the old name inside you — something like "the one nobody wanted", "the one who never does anything well" — and swap it for a sentence in which God says who you are. Say which sentence you are swapping it for.

13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — tell him the one thing you are burying, and ask him to check with you once this week whether you have done it. Say his name now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First: there is a man in the Bible who met God at a certain place when he was young, and thirty years later God told him to go back there. Second: before he went back he dug a hole and buried his household's idols in it, and he took a child named "son of sorrow" and renamed him "son of the right hand". Third: so I believe that your past can be entirely real and still not have to be your name. Write down now who you are going to tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the one thing you are going to bury, and the day you are going back to your Bethel. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord to bring us past merely commemorating him, and into actually handing something over.
